questions.question: In graph coverage testing, how is a 'test path' formally defined?

options.A: Any arbitrary sequence of vertices in the graph.
options.B: A path that starts at an initial node n0 ∈ N0 and ends at a final node nf ∈ Nf.
options.C: A cycle that visits every node in the graph at least twice.
options.D: A path containing only prime paths.

questions.explanation: A test path is a path that begins at an initial node (n0 ∈ N0) and terminates at a final/exit node (nf ∈ Nf). It corresponds to a complete execution trace of a test case.

questions.question: What does Node Coverage (NC) require?

options.A: Every reachable node in graph G must be visited by at least one test path.
options.B: Every edge and node must be visited simultaneously.
options.C: Every node must be visited in every test case.
options.D: Every node must be visited an even number of times.

questions.explanation: Node Coverage requires the set of test requirements TR to contain every reachable node in the graph G. Test paths must visit each node at least once.

questions.question: What is the formal definition of Edge Coverage (EC)?

options.A: TR contains each reachable path of length up to 1, inclusive, in G.
options.B: TR contains all cycles of length 2.
options.C: TR contains all paths between initial nodes and final nodes.
options.D: TR contains each node with in-degree greater than 1.

questions.explanation: Edge Coverage requires that TR contains each reachable path of length up to 1 inclusive in G, which corresponds to visiting every reachable edge (and isolated node).

questions.question: Does Edge Coverage (EC) always subsume Node Coverage (NC)?

options.A: No, Node Coverage subsumes Edge Coverage.
options.B: Yes, visiting every edge (and reachable path of length up to 1) guarantees visiting every reachable node.
options.C: Only in directed acyclic graphs.
options.D: Only when the graph has no loops.

questions.explanation: Edge coverage subsumes node coverage because every reachable node (except isolated nodes, which have a path of length 0) is an endpoint of some reachable edge.

questions.question: What is a 'simple path' in a graph G?

options.A: A path that contains no loops at all.
options.B: A path from node ni to nj where no node appears more than once, except that the first and last nodes may be identical.
options.C: A path containing at most two nodes.
options.D: A path that executes in constant time O(1).

questions.explanation: A path is simple if no node appears more than once, with the single exception that the first and last nodes may be the same (forming a simple cycle).

questions.question: What is a 'prime path'?

options.A: A path whose length is a prime number.
options.B: A simple path that does not appear as a proper subpath of any other simple path.
options.C: A path containing only initial and final nodes.
options.D: A path that visits every node in the graph.

questions.explanation: A prime path is a maximal simple path: a simple path that is not a proper subpath of any other simple path in the graph.

questions.question: What is the key difference between touring with 'sidetrips' versus touring with 'detours'?

options.A: A sidetrip leaves path p at node ni and returns to node ni; a detour leaves at ni and returns to a successor node ni+1.
options.B: Sidetrips are allowed only in trees; detours are allowed only in DAGs.
options.C: Detours return to the same node; sidetrips return to a predecessor node.
options.D: There is no difference; both terms are strictly synonymous.

questions.explanation: Touring with sidetrips means departing from node ni to visit a cycle and returning to the exact same node ni. Touring with detours means departing at ni and returning to ni+1 (the next node in the subpath).

questions.question: Why is Complete Path Coverage (CPC) generally impossible or impractical for programs containing loops?

options.A: Because loops can execute an unbounded number of iterations, making the number of paths infinite.
options.B: Because loops cannot be represented in a Control Flow Graph.
options.C: Because CPC only applies to specification graphs.
options.D: Because CPC violates the definition of a test path.

questions.explanation: If a graph contains a cycle/loop, an infinite number of paths can be constructed by iterating the loop different numbers of times. Hence, CPC is impossible to satisfy with a finite test suite.

questions.question: What is the requirement for Edge-Pair Coverage (EPC)?

options.A: TR contains each reachable path of length up to 2, inclusive, in G.
options.B: Every test case must execute exactly two edges.
options.C: Every edge must be paired with every other edge in the graph.
options.D: Edges must be visited in pairs of forwards and backwards traversals.

questions.explanation: Edge-Pair Coverage requires TR to contain every reachable path of length up to 2 (i.e. every pair of adjacent edges) in G.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly displays the subsumption hierarchy among structural graph criteria?

options.A: Node Coverage → Edge Coverage → Edge-Pair Coverage → Prime Path Coverage
options.B: Complete Path Coverage → Prime Path Coverage → Edge-Pair Coverage → Edge Coverage → Node Coverage
options.C: Prime Path Coverage → Complete Path Coverage → Edge Coverage
options.D: Edge-Pair Coverage → Prime Path Coverage → Node Coverage

questions.explanation: CPC subsumes PPC; PPC subsumes EPC; EPC subsumes EC; EC subsumes NC. (Where A → B denotes A subsumes B).

questions.question: Consider a graph with nodes {1, 2, 3} and edges (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 2). What is the path [2, 3, 2]?

options.A: A prime path of length 2.
options.B: A simple path that is not prime.
options.C: Not a simple path because node 2 is repeated.
options.D: An infeasible path in all graphs.

questions.explanation: [2, 3, 2] is a simple path because the only repeated node is the first and last (a simple cycle). It cannot be extended without repeating an internal node, so it is a prime path of length 2.

questions.question: Can a path of length 0 be a prime path?

options.A: Yes, if a node has no incoming and no outgoing edges (an isolated node).
options.B: No, prime paths must have length at least 1.
options.C: No, length 0 paths are not paths.
options.D: Yes, every single node in any graph is always a prime path.

questions.explanation: A path of length 0 is a single node [n]. If n has no edges connected to it, [n] cannot be extended to any longer simple path, making it a maximal simple path (prime path).

questions.question: If test path p is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], does p tour subpath [2, 3, 4] directly?

options.A: Yes, [2, 3, 4] is a subpath of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
options.B: No, because p starts at 1, not 2.
options.C: No, it only tours [2, 3, 4] with sidetrips.
options.D: Only if [2, 3, 4] is a prime path.

questions.explanation: A test path p tours a subpath q directly if q is a contiguous subpath of p. Here, [2, 3, 4] appears contiguously in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

questions.question: Why does Prime Path Coverage (PPC) avoid the problem of infinite paths in graphs with loops?

options.A: Because prime paths are simple paths, and by definition simple paths cannot loop indefinitely.
options.B: Because PPC deletes all loops from the graph before testing.
options.C: Because loops can only be traversed backwards under PPC.
options.D: Because PPC limits test cases to at most 10 paths.

questions.explanation: Simple paths visit each node at most once (except possibly start and end nodes of a cycle). Therefore, on any finite graph, the length of simple paths is strictly bounded by |N| + 1, making the set of prime paths finite.

questions.question: What is Complete Round Trip Coverage (CRTC)?

options.A: TR contains all round-trip paths (cycles of length >= 1) in G.
options.B: TR requires touring each round-trip path of length 0.
options.C: TR contains at least one round-trip path for each node.
options.D: TR requires executing the program until it reboots.

questions.explanation: Complete Round Trip Coverage requires that TR contains all round-trip paths (paths of length 1 or more that start and end at the same node) in G.

questions.question: What is Simple Round Trip Coverage (SRTC)?

options.A: TR contains at least one round-trip path for each reachable node that is the start of a round-trip path.
options.B: TR contains all simple paths of length 1.
options.C: TR requires round trips to be executed in zero time.
options.D: TR contains all paths with no round trips.

questions.explanation: Simple Round Trip Coverage requires TR to contain at least one round-trip path for each reachable node that can begin a round-trip path.

questions.question: Does Prime Path Coverage subsume Complete Round Trip Coverage?

options.A: Yes, prime paths include all simple cycles, but not non-simple round trips.
options.B: No, because CRTC can include round trips that are not simple paths.
options.C: Yes, PPC subsumes all path coverage criteria.
options.D: Neither can be compared.

questions.explanation: CRTC requires all round trips, including those formed by composing multiple cycles. Prime paths only include simple cycles; thus PPC does not subsume CRTC.

questions.question: If a graph has no cycles (is a Directed Acyclic Graph - DAG), what is the relationship between Prime Path Coverage and Complete Path Coverage?

options.A: PPC is equivalent to CPC for all paths from initial to final nodes.
options.B: CPC is still infinite.
options.C: PPC generates fewer paths than Edge Coverage.
options.D: PPC cannot be applied to DAGs.

questions.explanation: In an acyclic graph, every path is a simple path. Prime paths starting at initial nodes and ending at final nodes correspond precisely to all complete paths in the DAG.

questions.question: Which of the following test requirements can be infeasible?

options.A: Only node coverage requirements.
options.B: Test requirements in any criterion if the semantics of the code make that path or condition unreachable.
options.C: Only edge-pair coverage requirements.
options.D: Infeasible test requirements never occur in software testing.

questions.explanation: Infeasibility arises when control flow structures allow a theoretical path in the graph, but program semantics (contradictory branch conditions, impossible variable values) make executing that path impossible.

questions.question: In best-effort touring, if a prime path cannot be toured directly due to infeasibility, what does the tester attempt?

options.A: Tour the path with sidetrips or detours.
options.B: Delete the node from the program.
options.C: Declare 100% coverage immediately.
options.D: Crash the compiler.

questions.explanation: When touring directly is infeasible, touring with sidetrips is permitted as a relaxed (best-effort) requirement to visit the critical segments of the subpath.
